passage: The application portal closed on Friday at noon, and Nitin still had not emailed Dr Maria Fernandes for a reference. It was a four-line email. He had drafted it in his head on Monday. But she had been his thesis guide, and he had submitted that thesis three weeks late. Every time he opened a blank message, he pictured her reading his name and sighing. So he answered other mails, cleaned his inbox, booked his train to Nagpur for his cousin's engagement. On Thursday night, on that train, the network came and went between stations. At Wardha the signal jumped to full. His stomach dropped, and he typed it fast, without polishing: could she write a reference, the deadline, thank you. Sent. He stared out of the window at the dark fields. Forty minutes later, near the next station, her reply came: "Of course, Nitin. Happy to."

qa.q: Where did Nitin finally send the email?
qa.a: On the train, when the signal jumped to full at Wardha.

qa.q: Why did such a short email feel so hard for Nitin to send?
qa.a: He dreaded Dr Fernandes's reaction because his thesis had been three weeks late, so the fear of her disappointment made a four-line task feel huge.

qa.q: What could Nitin try next time a small email feels this heavy?
qa.a: He could write it quickly without polishing, the way he did at Wardha, and send it early in the day before the dread grows.

qa.q: How might Dr Fernandes see Nitin's request?
qa.a: She seems to see it as a simple, welcome request and answers warmly within forty minutes, with no sign of the judgement Nitin feared.

grounding: It shows an adult delaying a short but important email for days because he dreads the reply, though the task itself is small.

passage: On Monday afternoon, in the Andheri office, Seema found the error: in the report she had sent the client last week, two columns of survey figures were swapped. Lalit, her team lead, had signed off on it because he trusted her. She opened a new email. Hi Lalit, I found a mistake. She deleted it. On Tuesday she reorganised the shared folder instead, colour-coding every file. On Wednesday she stayed late fixing the spreadsheet perfectly, so at least the fix would be ready. Every time she thought of pressing send, she heard Lalit's quiet "hmm" from a meeting months ago and felt her face burn. By Thursday morning the draft was still three lines long. Then the client's assistant emailed Lalit a question about the swapped columns. Seema watched Lalit read it at his desk across the room, and her hands went cold on the keyboard.

qa.q: What error did Seema find in the report?
qa.a: Two columns of survey figures were swapped.

qa.q: Why did Seema keep deleting the email and reorganising files instead?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and scared of Lalit's reaction, remembering his quiet 'hmm', so busy work felt safer than facing that moment.

qa.q: What went wrong, and what could fix it next time?
qa.a: The delay let the client find the mistake first; sending a short, honest email on Monday with the fix attached would have been kinder to everyone, including Seema.

qa.q: How might Lalit feel learning about the error from the client?
qa.a: Lalit might feel caught off guard and a little let down, since he trusted Seema and would rather have heard it from her first.

grounding: It shows an adult putting off a brief, important email for days because she dreads the reaction, until the delay makes things worse.

passage:
"Asif, it's been five days. Did you reply to the Kolkata company?"
"Not yet, Trisha. I'm going to."
"You told me you're not taking the offer. So it's a no. What's the problem?"
"The recruiter was so nice. She called me twice. If I say no, she'll think I wasted her time."
"She'll think that more if you disappear."
"I know. Every time I open the laptop I feel sick. So I watch videos instead."
"How long would the email be?"
"Four lines? Five?"
"Five lines, and you've carried it around for five days."
Asif laughed, a bit shakily. "When you say it like that..."
"Open it. I'll sit here. Thank her, say you're declining, wish her well."
He typed with Trisha reading over his shoulder. His finger hovered, then pressed send.
"That's it?" he said.
"That's it."
Twenty minutes later: "Thanks for letting us know, Asif. All the best!"

qa.q: How many days had Asif not replied to the Kolkata company?
qa.a: It had been five days.

qa.q: What was Asif afraid of, and how did it feel from the inside?
qa.a: He was anxious that the kind recruiter would think he had wasted her time, so opening the laptop made him feel sick and videos felt like relief.

qa.q: How did Trisha help Asif get started?
qa.a: Trisha shrank the task by asking how long the email would be, sat with him, and gave him three simple points to write.

qa.q: How might the recruiter see Asif's reply compared with silence?
qa.a: The recruiter seems glad to have a clear answer, replying warmly within twenty minutes, whereas silence would have left them waiting and unsure.

grounding: It shows an adult postponing a short, important email for days because he dreads the response, until a friend helps him see how small the task is.

passage:
Sunday. Chetan had not touched his design portfolio for three weeks. He opened the folder, saw the half-finished case study, and heard himself mutter, "Useless. Every other architect my age has this done." He closed the laptop and scrolled until two in the morning, feeling worse.

Wednesday. Yamini, his flatmate, found him staring at the closed laptop. "What would you say if I'd delayed this?" she asked. He thought. "I'd say you had a hard month, and just do five minutes." "So say it to yourself." He did, out loud, feeling silly. Then he set a timer for five minutes and wrote one caption.

The next Monday. The timer was on again, but Chetan had stopped watching it. He had finished two case studies over the weekend. When he slipped, he said, "Okay, today was messy," and opened the folder anyway.

qa.q: How long had Chetan not touched his design portfolio?
qa.a: For three weeks.

qa.q: How did Chetan feel after calling himself useless on Sunday?
qa.a: He felt worse, ashamed and discouraged, and escaped into scrolling until two in the morning instead of working.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Chetan, and why?
qa.a: Speaking to himself as kindly as he would to a friend and committing to five minutes worked, because it removed the guilt that kept him avoiding the folder.

qa.q: How does Yamini help without doing the work for Chetan?
qa.a: Yamini asks a question that lets Chetan find the kind words himself, so the change comes from him rather than a lecture.

grounding: It shows an adult who stops berating himself for delay, forgives it and commits to five minutes, and then keeps working over the following days.

passage: Avni, you think I was always this organised? Let me tell you about my first year as a lab assistant. My report on the soil samples was due, and I kept not writing it. Each morning I'd look at the notebook and tell myself, what kind of scientist can't write one report? Then I'd feel so rotten that I'd go and wash glassware instead. Two weeks of that. One evening old Dr Pillai found me scrubbing beakers that were already clean. He didn't scold. He said, "Leela, beti, you're punishing yourself into doing nothing. Forgive yesterday. Give it five minutes." I nearly cried, and then I sat down and wrote the title and one paragraph. The next day, five minutes became an hour. I finished that week. When I catch myself calling myself names now, I remember him and the clean beakers.

qa.q: What was Leela washing when Dr Pillai found her?
qa.a: She was scrubbing beakers that were already clean.

qa.q: Why did Leela keep washing glassware instead of writing the report?
qa.a: Calling herself a poor scientist made her feel so rotten and guilty that avoiding the notebook felt like relief.

qa.q: At which point in the story did things turn, and why?
qa.a: The turn came when Leela took Dr Pillai's advice to forgive yesterday and give it five minutes; without the guilt, starting felt possible and she kept going.

qa.q: How did Dr Pillai seem to see Leela's struggle?
qa.a: Dr Pillai saw that her harshness toward herself was the real block, not laziness, and responded gently instead of scolding.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how forgiving her own delay and committing to five minutes helped her return to work, when self-blame had only fed avoidance.

passage: The electricity in their Lucknow lane went off every afternoon at three, and both Rehana and her cousin Vasudha had online course assignments overdue by a week. They sat on the same terrace, laptops on battery. Vasudha opened hers and groaned. "I'm so pathetic. I had seven days." She closed it again and started listing everything wrong with herself. Rehana felt the same sting. She had delayed too. But she took a breath and said, quietly, "Okay. I got behind. That happens. Five minutes, then I'll see." The battery icon showed forty minutes left. She wrote the first question's answer in five, then kept going. When the power came back at six, Rehana had finished half. Vasudha had watched three short videos about productivity and felt worse than before. "How did you even start?" she asked. "I stopped yelling at myself," Rehana said.

qa.q: When did the electricity go off in their Lucknow lane?
qa.a: Every afternoon at three.

qa.q: What was Rehana feeling when she saw her own delay, and how did she handle it?
qa.a: She felt the same guilty sting as Vasudha, but she forgave herself calmly and committed to five minutes, which let her start.

qa.q: What small step could help Vasudha tomorrow?
qa.a: Vasudha could say something kind about the delay, like Rehana did, and set a five-minute goal on one question instead of listing her faults.

qa.q: How is Vasudha affected by berating herself?
qa.a: Vasudha stays stuck, closes the laptop, and ends the afternoon feeling worse than before, with no work done.

grounding: It shows two adults with the same delay: one forgives herself and commits to five minutes and continues, the other berates herself and stays stuck.

passage: Saurabh, you ask why I still fall asleep the moment my head touches the pillow? Listen. When I was a girl of nine, in our village near Nashik, my Aaji had one rule. After dinner, wash feet at the tap, brush with the neem stick, then lie on the mat for her story. Every night, same order. At first I fought it. I wanted to play marbles. But after some weeks, my feet walked to the tap on their own. Once, at my uncle's wedding, the lights and drums went on till late. Still, I washed my feet at a strange tap, brushed, and lay beside Aaji. Before her story ended, I was asleep. That is Ganga's secret, beta: the steps carry you.

qa.q: What did Ganga use to brush her teeth as a child?
qa.a: A neem stick.

qa.q: How did young Ganga feel about the bedtime rule at first, and later?
qa.a: At first she felt resistant and wanted to play marbles; later the steps felt so natural that she felt calm and fell asleep easily even at a noisy wedding.

qa.q: What choice in the story made the routine stick?
qa.a: Aaji keeping the same order every night, even on busy days, made the steps automatic for young Ganga.

qa.q: How might Aaji have felt when young Ganga fell asleep during the story at the wedding?
qa.a: Aaji may have felt pleased and tender, seeing that the routine now worked even in a noisy, unfamiliar place.

grounding: It shows an elder recalling how, as a child, the same bedtime steps each night made brushing, story and sleep follow automatically.

passage: The school camp at the hill station had one problem: rain. It drummed on the tents all evening, and the boys in Pranav's tent were too excited to settle. Pranav, who was nine, felt jumpy too. But at nine o'clock something odd happened. His hands found his toothbrush in the bag. At home, brushing came right before Papa's story and then lights off. So he stood under the tent flap, rinsing into the wet grass. Tenzin sir, the camp teacher, saw him. "Ready for sleep already?" Pranav nodded, surprised at himself. He lay down and asked Tenzin sir for a story. By the second page, the rain sounded far away, and his eyes were closing.

qa.q: What was drumming on the tents all evening?
qa.a: The rain was drumming on the tents.

qa.q: Why was Pranav surprised at himself when he started brushing?
qa.a: He had felt jumpy and excited, yet his hands reached for the toothbrush on their own because the routine was so familiar, which left him surprised and then calm.

qa.q: How could Tenzin sir help the other children settle?
qa.a: Tenzin sir could set a simple, repeated order each camp night, like brushing, a story and lights off, so the steps start to feel familiar.

qa.q: What is it like for Tenzin sir to see Pranav ready for sleep in all the noise?
qa.a: Tenzin sir seems pleasantly surprised and happy to help, since one calm child makes the tent easier to settle.

grounding: It shows a child whose repeated bedtime steps at home carried over automatically at a noisy, rainy camp.

passage: In their Chennai flat, Suraj had the same bedtime every night: brush teeth at half past eight, climb into bed, Amma Sunaina reads a chapter, lights out. He was ten and said he was too old for stories, but he never skipped them. Then on Wednesday Amma had to travel for work. Appa was on the phone with the office. At half past eight, Suraj looked up from his puzzle, went to the bathroom, and brushed without anyone telling him. He climbed into bed and opened the storybook himself. He read the chapter aloud, quietly, the way Amma did. Halfway through, he yawned. When Appa came in, the book was open on the blanket and Suraj was asleep.

qa.q: What time did Suraj brush his teeth every night?
qa.a: At half past eight.

qa.q: What might Suraj have felt when he went to brush without being told?
qa.a: He probably felt a little lonely without Amma but also steady and grown-up, because the familiar steps told him what came next.

qa.q: What can parents learn from Suraj's evening?
qa.a: Keeping the same order and time for bedtime steps can make them feel automatic, so a child can follow them even when routines are disrupted.

qa.q: How might Appa feel finding Suraj asleep with the book?
qa.a: Appa might feel surprised, touched and a little guilty for being on the phone, but glad the routine held on its own.

grounding: It shows a child whose bedtime steps repeated at the same time made brushing, story and sleep follow automatically, even without his mother home.

subtype: Reaching for the phone when bored [Actor]
passage: The bus to Hoshangabad was late again, and the tea stall at the village stop had run out of milk. Kamal, fifteen, sat on the bench with his school bag. He took out his phone. Scrolled. A cricket clip, a cooking reel, a meme his cousin sent. He put it back. Twenty seconds later, a buffalo cart passed, and his hand was already in his pocket. He didn't remember deciding. His sister Rashmi, sitting beside him with her notebook, counted out loud. "Six times, Kamal. Since the tea man left." "No way." "Six." He laughed, but felt a little strange. When the bus finally came, he couldn't tell her a single thing he'd seen.

qa.q: Where was Kamal waiting?
qa.a: At the village bus stop, on the bench, waiting for the bus to Hoshangabad.

qa.q: Why did Kamal feel strange when Rashmi counted six times?
qa.a: He felt uneasy and a bit embarrassed, because he couldn't remember deciding to pick up the phone even once; each pause just led to his hand reaching for it.

qa.q: What small step could Kamal try at the bus stop?
qa.a: He could keep the phone in his school bag instead of his pocket, so there is a pause before reaching, and try noticing the boredom first.

qa.q: How does Rashmi see Kamal's habit?
qa.a: Rashmi sees it clearly from outside, counting each reach, and seems amused but also curious whether he notices it.

grounding: It shows a teenager who reaches for the phone at every pause and scrolls without deciding, as boredom, scrolling and small novelty form a loop.

subtype: Reaching for the phone when bored [Actor]
passage: On Tuesday the tram in Helsinki stopped for eleven minutes because of snow on the tracks. Ulla, sixteen, pulled out her phone. Soo-ah, her friend from the exchange programme, watched her. Ulla scrolled a video, closed it, opened a photo app, closed it, opened the video app again. When the tram jerked forward, she put the phone away. When it stopped again at the next station, the phone was back in her hand before the doors had even opened. "Are you looking for something?" Soo-ah asked. Ulla blinked. "No. I just... I don't know." She held the phone, screen dark, as if it had jumped into her hand by itself. For the rest of the ride she felt fidgety, fingers tapping her knee, staring at the grey windows.

qa.q: How long did the tram stop because of snow?
qa.a: Eleven minutes.

qa.q: What does Ulla's fidgeting after putting the phone down suggest she was feeling?
qa.a: It suggests she felt restless and a little unsettled, as if the pause was uncomfortable without the quick novelty of the phone.

qa.q: What could Ulla try next time the tram stops?
qa.a: She could notice the itch of boredom and choose something on purpose, like chatting with Soo-ah or watching the street, instead of reaching automatically.

qa.q: How might Soo-ah see Ulla's habit?
qa.a: Soo-ah seems curious and a little puzzled, noticing a pattern that Ulla herself doesn't seem aware of.

grounding: It shows a teenager reaching for the phone at every pause without deciding, as boredom, scrolling and small novelty have become a loop.

subtype: Reaching for the phone when bored [Actor]
passage: The free period in the school library of Kendriya Vidyalaya was supposed to be reading time. Sarita, in Class 11, had her biology book open. Every time she reached the end of a paragraph, her hand slid to her bag, and the phone came out under the table. A short clip, a notification, a message from the class group. Back to the book. Another paragraph, another pause, another reach. Trisha, at the next chair, nudged her. "You've done that like twenty times." Sarita frowned. "I'm just checking." "Checking what?" Sarita opened her mouth and realised she didn't know. The page was the same as fifteen minutes earlier. When the bell rang she had read two pages and could not say what either was about.

qa.q: How many pages had Sarita read when the bell rang?
qa.a: She had read two pages.

qa.q: Why did Sarita frown and say 'I'm just checking'?
qa.a: She felt a little defensive and caught out, because the reaching felt normal to her, and she only realised she didn't know what she was checking when Trisha asked.

qa.q: What would you advise Sarita for the next free period?
qa.a: Keep the phone in the library locker or zipped deep in the bag, and when the urge comes at the end of a paragraph, note it and read one more paragraph first.

qa.q: What is it like for Trisha sitting next to Sarita?
qa.a: Trisha seems a bit amused and a bit distracted, noticing each reach and wanting to point out the pattern.

grounding: It shows a teenager who picks up the phone at every pause in reading without deciding to, as boredom and quick novelty form a loop.

passage: Kofi first noticed it on a rainy Thursday in their Manchester terrace. His daughter Dalia came in from school, dropped her bag, sat on the sofa, and the phone was out before her coat was off. By five she was still there, homework untouched. Kofi felt the usual lecture rising in his throat. He didn't give it. Instead he watched for a week. Every day, same sequence: sofa, phone, gone. On days she stopped at the kitchen table first to eat toast, she did some maths before the phone appeared. On Saturday he moved the charger from the sofa to the hallway and put a bowl of fruit and her pencil case on the table. "Try the table first this week," he said, no telling off. Dalia rolled her eyes but tried. By Wednesday she was finishing homework before settling on the sofa.

qa.q: Where did Kofi move the charger?
qa.a: From the sofa to the hallway.

qa.q: What was Kofi feeling when he held back the lecture?
qa.a: Kofi felt frustrated, with a lecture rising in his throat, but chose patience and curiosity to watch the pattern first.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Changing the setting, moving the charger and setting up the table, worked better than nagging because the sofa itself was the cue for the phone habit.

qa.q: How does Dalia seem to experience her dad's change?
qa.a: Dalia rolls her eyes at first, but because there's no telling off, she's willing to try, and it soon becomes part of her routine.

grounding: It shows a parent who notices that the after-school phone habit starts on the sofa and changes the setting instead of nagging.

passage: Every day after school, Nitin waited in the staff room at St Joseph's for his mother Bidisha to finish her last class. And every day, he sank into the old green sofa by the window, and the phone came out. By the time she was free at five-thirty, his homework was still zipped in his bag. Bidisha had scolded him twice. It had not helped. On Monday she stood at the staff room door and just watched. He sat. Phone. He never even looked at the table. The sofa did the deciding. The next day she spoke to the librarian and arranged a desk in the corner of the library, near the window he liked. "Wait for me there from now on," she said, plainly. On Friday she found him at that desk with his science notebook open and the phone face down beside it.

qa.q: Where did Nitin wait for his mother after school?
qa.a: In the staff room at St Joseph's.

qa.q: What was Bidisha feeling after scolding Nitin twice had not helped?
qa.a: Bidisha felt frustrated and a bit helpless, which is why she stopped scolding and watched instead.

qa.q: What could other parents take from Bidisha's approach?
qa.a: Instead of nagging, notice where the habit begins and change that place, such as offering a different seat or room for after-school time.

qa.q: How might Nitin feel about moving to the library desk?
qa.a: Nitin might feel relieved that there is no more scolding, and the new spot by a window he liked may make it easier to open his notebook.

grounding: It shows a parent noticing that her son's phone habit begins on the staff room sofa and changing his setting instead of scolding.

passage:
Dear Sabina,

You asked how things are with Hiba and the phone. Better, and not because I shouted.

I watched her for a week, pretending to read the paper. She walks in, throws her bag down, drops onto the sofa, and in two seconds she's scrolling. It isn't a choice. The sofa is the switch.

So on Sunday I moved the phone basket to the dining table, next to a plate of fruit. When she gets home, phones go in the basket, she eats at the table, and homework starts there. The sofa is for after.

She sulked for two days. Then on Thursday she said, "It's weird, I don't even miss it till later." I nearly dropped my tea 😄

Your advice about not nagging helped. Come see us soon.

Zainab

qa.q: Where did Zainab move the phone basket?
qa.a: To the dining table, next to a plate of fruit.

qa.q: How did Zainab feel when Hiba said she didn't miss the phone till later?
qa.a: Zainab felt surprised and delighted, nearly dropping the tea, after a week of patient watching.

qa.q: What would you suggest to another parent facing the same after-school habit?
qa.a: Watch where the habit starts, then change the setting, like a basket at the table, instead of arguing about willpower.

qa.q: What was it like for Hiba when the phone basket moved?
qa.a: Hiba sulked for two days at first, but soon found she didn't miss the phone until later.

grounding: It shows a parent noticing that Hiba's phone habit starts on the sofa and changing the setting instead of nagging.

passage:
Dear Rukmini akka,

Remember you asked me to notice what I do when exams get close? I did, and I'm a bit embarrassed.

Last week I watched myself. I'd open the statistics notes, see a formula I didn't understand, and my chest would get tight. Then I'd be in the kitchen before I knew it, standing at the biscuit tin. Two biscuits, a nice little calm. Back to the desk. Tight chest. Kitchen again.

So now I can see it has parts: the formula is the trigger, the tight chest is the craving for relief, the biscuit is the reward. And the relief only lasts about a minute.

I'm not banning biscuits. But I've put a glass of water and a sticky note on my desk: 'Stuck? Write the question down.'

I'll tell you how it goes.

Jaya

qa.q: What does Jaya say triggers the tight chest?
qa.a: Seeing a formula Jaya didn't understand in the statistics notes.

qa.q: Why do the biscuits feel so appealing to Jaya in that moment?
qa.a: The tight chest is uncomfortable, and the biscuit brings a quick calm, so it feels like relief even though it lasts only about a minute and Jaya feels embarrassed noticing it.

qa.q: How does naming the loop's parts help Jaya choose where to change it?
qa.a: Seeing the formula as the trigger lets Jaya put a new response right there, writing the question down, instead of trying to fight the craving later.

qa.q: How might Rukmini akka feel reading this letter?
qa.a: Rukmini akka will likely feel proud and pleased that Jaya took the advice seriously and noticed the pattern 🙂

grounding: It shows a student who notices that stress leads to snacking and brief relief, and uses the loop's parts to find where to change it.

passage: So, Anirban, you asked why I went quiet in the group chat last month. Honestly? It wasn't the chat. It was me. Every time the project group sent a message, like 'who's doing slide nine?', my stomach would twist. And my thumb would go straight to the video app. Ten minutes of funny cat clips, and I'd feel lighter. Then I'd go back, see more messages, twist again, back to cats. For days. I felt busy the whole time and did nothing. It was my sister who asked, 'What happens right before you open that app?' And I sat there and traced it: message, twist, cats, lighter, repeat. Once I saw the chain, I moved one link. Now when the twist comes, I reply with one line first, even if it's 'I'll take slide nine.' Then the cats. That's how Vidya got her project done.

qa.q: What did the project group message ask?
qa.a: It asked, 'who's doing slide nine?'

qa.q: Why did the video app feel so tempting to Vidya each time?
qa.a: Each group message made Vidya's stomach twist with stress, and the cat clips brought quick relief, so repeating it felt natural.

qa.q: What change did Vidya make, and why did it help?
qa.a: Vidya replied with one line first when the stress came, then watched the clips; changing that one link stopped the loop from swallowing whole days.

qa.q: How might the project group have seen Vidya's silence?
qa.a: They might have felt confused or annoyed, not knowing Vidya was caught in a stress loop and not simply ignoring them.

grounding: It shows a student whose stress leads to scrolling and brief relief, and who changes the loop once its parts are noticed.

passage:
Monday, week one. Saurabh's code crashed for the fourth time. He shoved his chair back, walked to the hostel shop, and came back with a packet of chips. Crunching, he felt calmer. Crash. Chips. Vijay, his roommate, raised an eyebrow at the growing pile of wrappers.

Thursday, week two. Vijay handed him a sticky note. "Write down what happens right before you get up." Saurabh rolled his eyes but did it. Error message. Hot face. Get up. Chips. Calm for five minutes. Error again. Looking at the note, he muttered, "It's the error, not hunger."

Tuesday, week four. The screen flashed red. Saurabh's hand reached for his wallet, then stopped. He stood, stretched, filled his water bottle at the cooler, and came back to read the error line out loud. It still stung. But the wrappers on his desk had stopped piling up.

qa.q: What did Saurabh bring back from the hostel shop?
qa.a: A packet of chips.

qa.q: Why did going for chips feel right to Saurabh when the code crashed?
qa.a: The error made his face hot with frustration, and crunching chips brought quick calm, so the relief made the pattern feel natural.

qa.q: How did writing the steps down help Saurabh change the loop?
qa.a: Seeing 'error, hot face, get up, chips' showed that the trigger was the error, not hunger, so he could swap the routine at that point for water and reading the error.

qa.q: How does Vijay see the change in his roommate?
qa.a: Vijay likely feels pleased and a little proud, since his sticky note helped Saurabh notice the loop.

grounding: It shows a student whose stress triggers snacking for brief relief, and who changes the routine once he notices the loop's parts, across several weeks.

passage: Nandini lives across the corridor from me in the postgraduate hostel. At the start of term, she announced she would run every morning. The first week, I didn't see her run once. Then, one evening, I noticed her running shoes placed neatly beside her bed, socks tucked inside, and a note on the wall: 10 minutes. That's all. Next morning, at six, I heard her door. Through the window I saw her jog slowly around the hostel lawn and come back, still yawning. Twelve minutes, maybe. She did it again the next day, and the next. By the third week the note still said ten, but she was often gone for half an hour. I asked her once why only ten. She laughed. "Because I can't argue with ten, Gautam."

qa.q: What did Nandini place beside her bed?
qa.a: Her running shoes, placed neatly, with socks tucked inside.

qa.q: What might Gautam feel watching Nandini's routine grow?
qa.a: Gautam seems curious and quietly impressed, noticing the small changes and asking why the note only said ten.

qa.q: What can Gautam learn from Nandini for a habit of their own?
qa.a: Gautam could make the first step easy to reach and set a tiny target, so starting doesn't require a big effort each morning.

qa.q: How does Nandini explain her own approach?
qa.a: Nandini says ten minutes is too small to argue with, so she feels less resistance and starts without a battle.

grounding: It shows, through a hostel neighbour's eyes, a student who lays out running shoes by the bed and sets a ten-minute target, helping the habit survive its first weeks.

passage:
Week one, a Sunday night. Jeevan wanted to start running before college. Kamal, his roommate, watched him put his running shoes right by the bed, socks inside, water bottle next to them. "Only ten minutes," Jeevan said. "That's it." On Monday he stepped straight from the bed into the shoes and jogged around the colony park, grumbling. Ten minutes, done.

Week two, a rainy Thursday. The alarm rang and Jeevan groaned. But the shoes were right there, and ten minutes seemed silly to skip. He ran under the tin roofs of the lane and came back soaked, laughing.

passage: Ritu, you think running came easily to me? Arre, sit down. I was a thin girl then, in my second year at college in Guwahati. I tried to start running three times. Each time I set my alarm for five and planned five kilometres. Each time I lasted maybe four days. The fourth time, my roommate Sunanda said, "Why do you make it so heavy? Just put your shoes by your bed and go for ten minutes." I thought it was a joke. But I did it. Shoes by the bed, socks inside. Ten minutes around the hostel. Some days I came back after exactly ten and felt a bit silly. But I never skipped, because it was so small. By the second month I was running forty minutes without trying. That's how Binita became the one who wakes the whole family for a morning walk now.

passage: The phone calls from parents always came at the end of the school day in Sirsi, and they always left Devika tense. For months, after each call, she sat in the staff room and scrolled through news until the bus came, feeling worse. She had tried deleting the app twice. Both times it was back within a week. In June she tried something else. When a call ended, she kept the same pause, but walked out to the neem tree in the school courtyard and breathed slowly, counting ten breaths. In a small notebook, she drew a tick for each walk and a cross for each scroll. Farida, the maths teacher, noticed her standing under the tree. "Meditating?" "Something like that." By August, the notebook had many more ticks than crosses, and Devika was catching the bus with her shoulders down.

passage: Fatima worked the customer complaints line at a furniture company in Warsaw. After a hard call, her hand went to her phone, and she'd scroll until her supervisor coughed. She had tried locking the phone in her drawer. Then she just sat staring at the drawer, tense and irritable. Marek, who sat opposite, mentioned that he stood at the window after bad calls. So Fatima tried it: call ends, headset off, walk to the window, three slow breaths, look at the trams. Back. On a sticky note, she kept a tally: window or phone. On the first Friday, it was four windows and seven phones. By the third Friday, eleven windows and two phones. "Still need a break," she told Marek. "Just a different one." He nodded. The trams below kept moving, and Fatima's shoulders felt a little looser.

qa.a: Keeping the same cue but swapping in the window and breathing worked, because it still gave her the break she needed, and the tally showed her progress.

grounding: It shows an adult who keeps the stressful cue but replaces scrolling with breathing at a window and tracks the result, meeting the same need for a break.

Vinita
